title: Why Does IPA Give Me a Headache? IPA Hangovers Explained
excerpt: Why IPAs hit harder than other beers: the real role of ABV, pour size, hops, histamine, and haze, plus how to enjoy IPAs without the next-day headache.
metaDescription: Why does IPA give you a headache? How ABV, pour size, hops, and histamine drive IPA hangovers, and simple ways to drink IPAs without the pain.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if IPAs give you a worse headache or hangover than other beers, the most likely reason is simply that you're drinking more alcohol than you think. A typical IPA is 6 to 7.5% alcohol, double IPAs often run 8 to 10% or more, and craft bars commonly pour them in 16-ounce glasses. One pint of a 7% IPA holds close to two standard drinks. Three of them and you've had the alcohol of five or six light lagers. Hops get the blame, but there is no good evidence that hops themselves cause hangovers for most people. Strength, serving size, drinking pace, and a few secondary factors (histamine, unfiltered haze, sleep loss, dehydration) explain most of what people feel.

**The quick fixes:** count IPAs as 1.5 to 2.5 drinks each depending on strength and pour size, switch to a session IPA (around 4 to 5%) or alternate with water, order a smaller pour when you're trying something strong, eat before and while you drink, and stop earlier than you would with lager. If you get a headache within an hour of a single small IPA, that's a different pattern, and it's worth reading the section on sensitivity below.

> **When to see a doctor.** A pounding head the morning after a few beers is common and usually passes within a day. **Get medical care if** you have a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, a headache with fever and a stiff neck, confusion, slurred speech, weakness or numbness on one side, vision loss, or a headache after a head bump while drinking. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or keeps vomiting and can't keep water down; those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. Also talk to a doctor if even one drink reliably triggers hives, wheezing, facial swelling, or a migraine, or if you find you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious every time you stop drinking. This article explains general research; it isn't a substitute for advice from someone who knows your health history.

## Why Does IPA Give Me a Headache?

Most people who ask this have noticed a real pattern: the night of IPAs feels fine, and the next morning is rough in a way a night of pilsners isn't. The pattern is real. The usual explanation ("I must be allergic to hops") usually isn't.

Here are the factors, roughly in order of how much they matter for most social drinkers.

### 1. More alcohol per glass than you're counting

This is the big one. In the US, one "standard drink" is about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which equals a 12-ounce beer at 5%. IPAs don't sit at 5%.

| Beer and pour | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|
| 12 oz light lager, 4.2% | about 0.8 |
| 12 oz regular lager, 5% | 1.0 |
| 12 oz session IPA, 4.5% | about 0.9 |
| 12 oz IPA, 7% | about 1.4 |
| 16 oz IPA, 7% | about 1.9 |
| 16 oz double IPA, 9% | about 2.4 |
| 16 oz triple IPA, 11% | about 2.9 |

*Formula: ounces x ABV ÷ 0.6. Craft ABVs vary a lot, so check the can or the tap list.*

So "I only had four beers" can mean four drinks or ten drinks, depending on what was in the glass. Hangover severity rises with how much alcohol you drink and how high your blood alcohol gets. When people compare an IPA night to a lager night by counting glasses, they're comparing very different doses.

### 2. Strong beers often get drunk at lager speed

A lager and a double IPA take roughly the same time to finish. If you drink one glass an hour either way, the IPA delivers up to two or three times as much alcohol per hour. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, often estimated at around one standard drink per hour for an average adult (it varies with body size, sex, genetics, and food). Anything faster than that piles up, and your blood alcohol climbs. Hoppy bitterness and juicy tropical fruit flavors also do a good job of hiding the taste of alcohol, so a 9% beer rarely tastes like a 9% beer.

### 3. Alcohol itself causes the headache

The hangover headache is mostly an alcohol effect, not a beer-style effect. A few things are going on at once:

- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more. Beer contains a lot of water, which helps, but at higher ABVs the diuretic effect still wins over a long night. Our guide to [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers this in more detail.
- **Blood vessel changes.** Alcohol widens blood vessels, which is one reason it's a well-known headache and migraine trigger.
- **Inflammation and acetaldehyde.** Your body breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before turning it into harmless acetate. Hangover research also links next-day symptoms to an inflammatory response from the immune system.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Short, broken sleep on its own causes headaches in many people.

For a deeper look at how each of these drives the pain, see [why alcohol gives you a headache](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025).

### 4. Secondary factors that can add on top

Once you account for alcohol dose, there are a few IPA-specific things that may matter for some people. The evidence for each is thinner, so treat these as possibilities rather than settled explanations.

- **Histamine and other biogenic amines.** Beer is fermented, and fermentation can produce histamine and tyramine. Levels vary widely between beers and breweries. Alcohol also slows the enzyme (diamine oxidase, or DAO) that breaks histamine down. In people with histamine intolerance, that combination can cause headaches, flushing, and a stuffy nose. There's no good evidence that IPAs are consistently higher in histamine than other beers, but it's a reasonable explanation for someone who reacts to a wide range of fermented drinks.
- **Unfiltered yeast and haze.** Hazy and New England IPAs are usually unfiltered, so they carry more yeast and suspended protein. Some drinkers report more bloating and gut upset with these beers. There's no good research tying haze to worse hangovers, though.
- **Added ingredients.** "Milkshake" IPAs often contain lactose, which bothers people who are lactose intolerant. Some hazy IPAs contain oats or wheat. These won't cause a headache directly for most people, but a churning stomach makes the morning worse.
- **Congeners.** These are by-products of fermentation that may contribute to hangovers. Darker spirits like bourbon tend to be higher in them than clear spirits. Beer generally sits in the lower-to-middle range, and there's no good data showing IPAs are unusually high. Our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains what's known.

## Are IPA Hangovers Worse Than Lager Hangovers?

Drink for drink, measured in actual alcohol, there's no good evidence that an IPA produces a worse hangover than a lager. Glass for glass, they very often do, because each glass carries more alcohol.

A fair test would be four 12-ounce lagers at 5% versus about three 12-ounce IPAs at 7%. Those are roughly equal doses of alcohol. Most people never make that comparison. They swap four lagers for four or five pints of IPA and then blame the hops.

If you want to check for yourself, try this: on an IPA night, add up your standard drinks using the formula above, and compare that number to a typical lager night. If the IPA night was much higher, you've found your answer. If the numbers are close and you still feel far worse, one of the sensitivity factors below may be involved. For a broader comparison of beer against wine and spirits, see our guide to [beer hangovers](/never-hungover/beer-hangover). If your main complaint is a pounding head rather than general misery, our guide to [beer headaches](/never-hungover/beer-headache) covers that side.

## Is It the Hops? What Hops Actually Do

Hops are the flowers of the *Humulus lupulus* plant. They give IPAs their bitterness and their piney, citrusy, or tropical aromas. They contain bitter acids (alpha acids, which become iso-alpha acids during boiling), essential oils like myrcene, and plant compounds such as xanthohumol.

What we know about hops and how you feel:

- **No good evidence of a hangover effect.** Researchers have studied hangovers in relation to alcohol dose, congeners, and genetics, but there's no good evidence that hop compounds at the levels found in beer cause next-day headaches in typical drinkers.
- **Hops have a long reputation as a mild sedative.** Hop extracts show up in some herbal sleep products, often paired with valerian. The evidence is modest, and the amounts in beer are small, but it's a reminder that "hops are toxic" isn't the right frame.
- **Hop sensitivity is real but uncommon.** Some people have allergic reactions to hops, most often documented in hop farm and brewery workers who handle the plant. Hops are in the same plant family as cannabis, and occasional cross-reactions have been reported. If you react to hoppy beers with hives, itching, wheezing, or swelling, that's an allergy question for a doctor, not a hangover question.

Heavily dry-hopped beers do contain far more hop material than a lager. If you consistently feel worse after very hoppy beers even at the same alcohol dose, it's reasonable to test that by switching to a less hoppy beer of the same strength for a few weeks and noticing whether anything changes.

## Why Do I Get a Headache From Just One IPA?

A headache within an hour or two of one small beer isn't a hangover. Hangovers show up after your blood alcohol has fallen, usually the next morning. A fast headache from a small amount points to a sensitivity of some kind. Common possibilities include:

- **Migraine.** Alcohol is one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers. If you get migraines, even modest amounts of any alcohol can set one off.
- **Histamine intolerance.** Headache, flushing, a runny or blocked nose, and sometimes hives soon after drinking can point to trouble clearing histamine. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) walks through the signs.
- **Alcohol flush reaction.** Some people, especially many of East Asian descent, carry a gene variant that slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde. They tend to flush red, feel their heart race, and get a headache after small amounts of any alcohol.
- **Medication interactions.** Some medicines react badly with alcohol, including certain antibiotics, some diabetes drugs, and others. Check the label or ask a pharmacist.

If this sounds like you, our page on [getting a headache after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) goes into each cause, and a doctor can help you sort out which one applies.

## Double IPA, Hazy IPA, and Session IPA: How the Styles Compare

"IPA" now covers a big family of beers. They differ a lot in strength, which matters more than any other difference for how you'll feel tomorrow.

### Double and triple IPAs

Double (or imperial) IPAs typically sit around 8 to 10% alcohol, and triple IPAs can go higher. That's close to the strength of some wines, served in beer-sized portions. A single 16-ounce pour of a 10% beer is almost three standard drinks. Many breweries serve these in smaller glasses for exactly that reason. If you want to drink them, treat each one as two or three drinks and plan your night around that.

### Hazy and New England IPAs

Hazy IPAs are often 6 to 8% alcohol, soft, and very easy to drink, which can make them sneakier than a sharply bitter West Coast IPA. They're also usually unfiltered. Some drinkers say they feel more bloated after them. If hazies leave you feeling worse, try counting the alcohol first, then try a filtered beer of the same strength to see if the difference holds.

### West Coast IPAs

These are clearer, drier, and more bitter, usually in the 6.5 to 7.5% range. The bitterness can slow some people down a little, but the alcohol content is still well above a lager.

### Session IPAs

Session IPAs are hoppy beers brewed at around 4 to 5% alcohol. If you enjoy the flavor of IPAs but want a lighter morning, this is the simplest swap you can make. You keep the hops and drop the alcohol to lager levels.

### Non-alcoholic IPAs

Hoppy non-alcoholic beers have improved a lot and are widely available. In the US, "non-alcoholic" can still mean up to 0.5% alcohol, which is far too little to cause a hangover for most people. If you still get a headache from a non-alcoholic IPA, that points toward a sensitivity to something other than alcohol and is worth mentioning to a doctor.

## How to Drink IPAs Without the Headache

None of these steps makes a hangover impossible, but each one reduces how much alcohol hits your system or how hard your body takes it.

### Before you start

- **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach, especially protein and fat, slows how fast alcohol is absorbed and lowers your peak blood alcohol.
- **Check the ABV.** Craft tap lists almost always show it. Decide in advance how many standard drinks you're comfortable with, then convert that into glasses.
- **Start hydrated.** Showing up already thirsty after a long day or a workout makes things worse.

### While you're drinking

- **Order smaller pours of strong beers.** Many taprooms offer 5, 8, or 10-ounce pours. A 10-ounce glass of 9% beer is about 1.5 drinks instead of 2.4 for a pint.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between beers slows your pace and offsets some of the fluid loss.
- **Put the session beer first or last.** Starting with a 4.5% session IPA lets you settle in without front-loading alcohol. Finishing with one, or with a non-alcoholic IPA, keeps you in the social rhythm without adding much.
- **Don't save the strongest beer for the end.** Late-night double IPAs hit when your judgment is already loosened and your blood alcohol is already high.
- **Watch the flights.** Tasting flights look small, but four 5-ounce pours of 7 to 10% beers add up to roughly two to three standard drinks.

### Before bed

- **Drink a glass or two of water.** Not a gallon. Enough to start the night hydrated.
- **Skip the extra nightcap.** The last drink of the night does the most damage to your sleep and your morning.
- **Give yourself time to sleep.** A full night of sleep after drinking won't undo the alcohol, but short sleep reliably makes the headache worse.

For a fuller playbook, see our main guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## What to Do the Morning After

If you already have the IPA headache, here's what tends to help most:

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is fine. An electrolyte drink can help if you've been sweating, vomiting, or have diarrhea.
2. **Eat something simple.** Toast, eggs, rice, bananas, or soup can settle your stomach and bring up low blood sugar.
3. **Consider a pain reliever carefully.** Ibuprofen tends to help hangover headaches but can irritate the stomach, so take it with food. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, so avoid stacking it on a heavy night of drinking and never take more than the label allows. Read our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before choosing.
4. **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another beer pushes the hangover later rather than fixing it.
5. **Rest and wait.** Most hangovers fade within about 24 hours. Caffeine can help with a headache if you're a regular coffee drinker, but too much can make dehydration and jitteriness worse.

Our page on [fast hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers more options and what the evidence says about each one.

## Could It Be Something Other Than the Beer?

Sometimes the IPA is a bystander. A few things that often travel with a big craft beer night can also cause a headache:

- **Salty, heavy food.** Bar snacks and late-night pizza can leave you thirstier.
- **Caffeine withdrawal.** If you slept in and missed your usual morning coffee, that alone can cause a headache.
- **Loud, smoky, or crowded places.** Noise, smoke, and late nights add up.
- **Mixing drinks.** A couple of IPAs followed by shots raises your total alcohol quickly. The old "beer before liquor" rhyme isn't really about order, as our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) guide explains; it's about total amount.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take when they drink. Research, mostly in animals and lab studies with limited human data, suggests it may support the body's breakdown of alcohol and acetaldehyde and may affect how alcohol acts on the brain. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it doesn't change the math on a 9% double IPA. Counting your drinks, eating, and pacing yourself matter more than any supplement.

If you'd like to try it as one part of a sensible plan, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist or doctor before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

IPAs give many people worse headaches mostly because they're stronger beers served in bigger glasses and drunk at the same pace as lighter ones. Hops are rarely the problem. Count each IPA as roughly 1.5 to 2.5 drinks, choose session IPAs or smaller pours when you want an easier morning, alternate with water, and eat first. If one small beer reliably triggers a headache, flushing, or hives, that's a sensitivity worth discussing with a doctor rather than something to push through.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does IPA give me a headache?**

Mostly because IPAs carry more alcohol than most beers. A typical IPA is 6 to 7.5% alcohol and double IPAs often run 8 to 10% or more, so a 16-ounce pint can hold two or more standard drinks. Alcohol causes headaches through fluid loss, blood vessel changes, inflammation, and poor sleep. Histamine, unfiltered yeast, and personal sensitivities can add to it for some people, but there is no good evidence that hops cause hangovers in most drinkers.

**Are IPA hangovers worse than other beer hangovers?**

Glass for glass, usually yes, because each IPA contains more alcohol. Drink for drink, measured in actual alcohol, there is no good evidence that IPAs cause worse hangovers than lagers. Comparing four pints of 7% IPA to four 12-ounce lagers at 5% is comparing very different amounts of alcohol.

**Am I allergic to hops?**

Probably not, if your only symptom is a next-day headache. True hop allergy is uncommon and tends to cause hives, itching, sneezing, wheezing, or swelling, often soon after drinking. It has mostly been documented in people who handle hops at work. If you get those symptoms from hoppy beers, see a doctor or allergist.

**Do double IPAs give worse hangovers?**

They often do, because they're so strong. A 16-ounce pour of a 9% double IPA holds about 2.4 standard drinks, and a 10% beer is closer to three. Treat each double IPA as two to three drinks, order smaller pours, and alternate with water.

**Do hazy IPAs cause worse hangovers?**

There's no good research showing that haze itself makes hangovers worse. Hazy IPAs are unfiltered and often very easy to drink at 6 to 8% alcohol, which can lead to drinking more alcohol than you realize. Some people also report more bloating from them, and milkshake-style hazies may contain lactose.

**Why do I get a headache after just one IPA?**

A headache within an hour or two of a single small beer usually isn't a hangover. Common causes include migraine (alcohol is a well-known trigger), histamine intolerance, an alcohol flush reaction, or a medication interaction. If it happens regularly, talk to a doctor.

**What is the best beer to avoid a hangover?**

A lower-alcohol beer is the simplest choice. Session IPAs (about 4 to 5%) keep the hoppy flavor at lager strength, and non-alcoholic IPAs contain too little alcohol to cause a hangover for most people. Eating first, pacing yourself, and drinking water between beers matter as much as the style you pick.

**Can DHM help with an IPA hangover?**

DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone, and it can't offset drinking several strong IPAs. If you try it, treat it as one part of a plan that includes counting drinks, eating, and hydrating.
